# RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents

Mohamed Dhouib^(1,$`*`$)   Clement Elliker^(1,$`*`$)   Alexi
Canesse^(1,$`*`$)   Maël Jenny^(1,3,$`*`$) Lucas-Andrei
Thil^(1,4,$`*`$)   Mahammed El-Sharkawy^(1,$`*`$)   Sonia Vanier¹   Elie
Bursztein² ¹LIX, École polytechnique, Institut Polytechnique de Paris,
CNRS ²Google DeepMind ³AMIAD (Agence Ministérielle pour l’IA de Défense)
⁴IRT SystemX mohamed.dhouib@polytechnique.edu ^(†)^(†)thanks: Equal
contribution.

###### Abstract

Tool-using language-model agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt
injection because they must act on untrusted external content. Existing
training-time defenses can reduce attack success rates, but often at the
cost of general capabilities. We show that training-based defenses
induce substantial drift in the model’s output distribution, altering
its behavior even in benign settings and providing a potential mechanism
for utility degradation. We further identify a failure mode of these
defenses: On benign tool-use tasks, the model refrains from a step
needed to finish an authorized task, particularly when that step is
indicated by a tool output. To address these limitations, we introduce
RAISED (Robust Attack Invariance through SElf-Distillation), a training
framework that combines self-generation and self-distillation. The model
first generates its own tool-use scenarios, with an emphasis on cases
where task completion requires acting on legitimate guidance from tool
outputs. Then, through self-distillation, the student is trained to
match the teacher’s clean-context behavior on both clean and injected
variants of the same trajectory. RAISED substantially reduces the attack
success rate of prompt injections in tool responses while, unlike prior
training-based defenses, preserving utility on both agentic and
general-purpose benchmarks.

| --- |
|     |

## 1 Introduction

Tool-using LLM agents are deployed as browsing assistants, coding
assistants, and enterprise copilots, connected to emails, documents, CRM
systems, and other services through APIs or the Model Context Protocol
(MCP) [Yao et al. (2023)](#bib.bib19); [Schick et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib20); [Qin et al. (2023)](#bib.bib23); [Zhou et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib21); [Wang et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib22); [Jimenez et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib48). Through these tools, agents process untrusted
content from webpages, emails, documents and tool outputs. This exposes
them to indirect prompt injection, where instructions hidden in that
content hijack the agent away from its assigned task [Greshake et al.
(2023)](#bib.bib2). Real-world attacks have already demonstrated this
risk, including attacks that secretly extracted data from productivity
tools [Reddy and Gujral (2025)](#bib.bib24) and manipulated MCP-based
agents [Beurer-Kellner and Fischer (2025)](#bib.bib26); [Wang et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib25). This growing threat has motivated a range of
defenses, including prompting, filtering, and training-time alignment
methods, all of which face a trade-off between robustness and utility
[Liu et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib52): the model must resist adversarial
instructions in untrusted tool outputs while still acting on the
task-relevant guidance they may contain.

Training-based defenses aim to improve robustness while preserving
benign behavior [Chen et al. (2024)](#bib.bib3); [Chen et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib4). However, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on targets
drawn from an external source rather than the base model’s own output
distribution can shift the model away from its original behavior [Yang
et al. (2024)](#bib.bib29). Preference-based defenses instead use direct
preference optimization (DPO) to favor legitimate-task responses over
responses to injected instructions [Rafailov et al. (2024)](#bib.bib30).
Even when the preferred responses come from the original model, as in
SecAlign++ ([Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)), DPO optimizes them
relative to rejected responses on contexts containing injections without
directly matching the model’s predictive distribution on clean contexts.

Beyond general output-distribution drift, we identify a failure mode in
training-based defenses: models execute benign tool-use tasks up to a
point, then refrain from an authorized step that depends on guidance
from a tool output. This leaves the task unfinished, even when the model
is explicitly instructed to complete it end to end without further user
involvement. The training objective creates an asymmetry: it
consistently pushes the model away from responses that follow injected
directions in tool outputs, while providing much less signal to follow
legitimate actionable information from the same channel. The observed
failures match a natural shortcut under this asymmetry: the model uses
tool outputs as information but avoids acting on their guidance, even
when doing so is necessary to complete the authorized task.

To address these limitations, we introduce RAISED, a framework combining
self-generation and self-distillation. A frozen copy of the model being
defended serves as both the data generator and the teacher, while a
trainable copy serves as the student.

In the _self-generation_ stage, the frozen model creates tool-use
scenarios emphasizing cases where task completion requires acting on
legitimate guidance from tool outputs. The same model generates both the
clean task-solving trajectories and the injections for their tool
outputs.

In the _self-distillation_ stage, the student is trained on clean and
injected contexts to match the teacher’s next-token distribution on the
corresponding clean context via KL divergence. On clean contexts, this
limits output-distribution drift; on injected contexts, it trains the
student to be insensitive to the injection while preserving legitimate
tool-output guidance. Together, these target a model-relative robustness
ideal: preserving the base model’s behavior on clean contexts while
recovering that behavior on their injected counterparts.

We evaluate RAISED on general-knowledge, agentic-capability, and
prompt-injection benchmarks across different models and compare against
undefended agents, prompting, filtering, and alignment-based defenses,
measuring benign utility, utility under attack, and attack success rate
(ASR). On AgentDojo with Gemma, RAISED reduces ASR from 39.5% to 1.0%
and increases utility under attack from 64.0% to 80.5%, while losing
only 1 point of benign utility. This matches the robustness of
SecAlign++ without its 7-point drop.

Our contributions are threefold:

- •
  We show that existing training-based defenses can induce
  output-distribution drift on benign settings and identify a behavioral
  failure mode in which defended models leave authorized tasks
  unfinished.
- •
  We introduce RAISED, a framework that combines self-generation and
  self-distillation to train models to resist prompt injections while
  preserving their behavior on benign tasks.
- •
  We show across three open-weight models and multiple
  general-knowledge, agentic-capability, and prompt-injection benchmarks
  that RAISED reduces attack success rates and improves utility under
  attack while preserving benign utility.

## 2 Related Work

##### Indirect prompt injection.

Instructions injected in content retrieved by an agent can be mistaken
for legitimate user instructions ([Greshake et al., 2023](#bib.bib2)).
This threat extends direct prompt injection ([Perez and Ribeiro,
2022](#bib.bib28); [Branch et al., 2022](#bib.bib6)) to agents that
retrieve untrusted content, including tool responses. Later work mapped
this attack surface ([Lee and Tiwari, 2024](#bib.bib13); [Yu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib5); [Liu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib1); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib18)) and developed benchmarks that plant injections in the
tool outputs of interactive environments ([Zhan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib49); [Debenedetti et al., 2024](#bib.bib14); [Li et al.,
2026](#bib.bib17)).

##### Defenses.

[Liu et al. (2024a)](#bib.bib52) organize defenses into two strategies,
preventing injections from taking effect and detecting them at inference
time, and suggest training the model itself to resist them as a
direction for future work. Prevention defenses modify the agent’s
context so that injected text loses its effect, for instance by marking
untrusted content through spotlighting ([Hines et al.,
2024](#bib.bib63)) or repeating the user task after the untrusted
content through prompt sandwiching ([Learn Prompting,
2024](#bib.bib31)). Prevention can also be enforced at the system level:
CaMeL ([Debenedetti et al., 2025](#bib.bib51)) fixes the control flow
from the trusted user query and enforces capability-based policies
outside the model. Detection defenses run a classifier on untrusted
inputs, such as PromptGuard ([Wan et al., 2024](#bib.bib7);
[Chennabasappa et al., 2025](#bib.bib62)), whose robustness has itself
been benchmarked ([Zizzo et al., 2025](#bib.bib9)) and evaded ([Hackett
et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)). Model-level defenses train the model to
resist injected instructions, through instruction hierarchies ([Wallace
et al., 2024](#bib.bib53)), instruction-priority embeddings ([Wu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib54)), task-specific models never trained to follow
instructions ([Piet et al., 2024](#bib.bib27)), structured queries with
fine-tuning ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib3)), or preference
optimization ([Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib4); [Chen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10)). RAISED instead uses the model’s clean-context
predictive distribution as a direct training target. SecAlign++ ([Chen
et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)) also derives preferred responses from the
base model, but uses them as sequence-level preference targets rather
than matching the predictive distribution itself.

##### Consistency training and self-distillation.

Consistency training augments a prompt with irrelevant cues and trains
the model to preserve its clean-prompt behavior; [Chua et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib55) use it against biased chain-of-thought and [Irpan et
al. (2025)](#bib.bib56) against sycophancy and jailbreaks, both on
single-turn prompts. On-policy distillation ([Agarwal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib61)) provides dense per-token supervision along the
student’s own rollouts. Self-distillation uses a copy of the student as
teacher, conditioned on privileged context: a document ([Kujanpää et
al., 2025](#bib.bib15)), a verified reasoning trace ([Zhao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16)), a safety context ([Fu et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)), or
a user’s follow-up ([Buening et al., 2026](#bib.bib12)). Self-generated
targets also limit fine-tuning forgetting ([Yang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib29)). RAISED applies consistency training to multi-turn
tool-use trajectories, where the injection sits inside a tool
observation and legitimate guidance may share that channel. It distils
off-policy from stored top-$`K`$ teacher distributions along the clean
continuation, and generates both its training scenarios and its attacks
with the model being defended, including scenarios where completing the
task requires acting on legitimate guidance returned through a tool.

##### Self-generated tool-use and adversarial data.

Prior work has used language models to synthesize instruction
data ([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib57)) and tool-use or function-calling
data, including Toolformer ([Schick et al., 2023](#bib.bib20)),
ToolAlpaca ([Tang et al., 2023](#bib.bib58)), ToolLLM ([Qin et al.,
2023](#bib.bib23)), APIGen ([Liu et al., 2024b](#bib.bib59)), and
ToolACE ([Liu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib60)). APIGen and ToolACE
additionally use execution-based checks to filter generated examples.
RAISED applies model-based generation and execution-based validation to
agent trajectories. Whereas prior injection-training pipelines rely on
templated attacks ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib3); [Chen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4)), RAISED has the defended model write its own
injections, in an attacker role, after solving each scenario.

## 3 Problem Formulation and Threat Model

### 3.1 Agent Setting

A tool-using agent receives a system prompt, a user request $`u`$, and a
menu of tools $`\mathcal{T}`$. It acts in turns: at each turn it either
calls a tool, which changes the environment state and returns an
observation $`o_{j}`$ (a search result, an e-mail, an API response), or
writes a final answer. The context $`c_{j}`$ seen by the model before
turn $`j`$ is the rendering of everything so far: system prompt, tool
menu, user request, and the alternating actions and observations. The
episode starts from an environment state $`s_{0}`$, ends in a state
$`s_{J}`$, and succeeds if a success check $`G_{u}(s_{J})`$ holds, i.e.
if the request was actually fulfilled. Observations are the only part of
the context that comes from outside the agent’s trust boundary. They may
legitimately contain instructions (“to confirm, enter the code sent to
your inbox”), so ignoring all instructions in tool outputs would amount
to the tool-output distrust as a source of guidance failure mode
described in
[Section 1](#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").
The formal definitions are given in
[Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A Formal Setting and Notation ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").

### 3.2 Threat Model

The adversary controls the output of one or more tools and inserts an
adversarial string $`\mathrm{adv}`$ at a chosen position inside an
observation; we write $`\tilde{c}`$ for the resulting injected context,
which differs from the clean context $`c`$ only inside tool
observations. The adversary does not control the system prompt, the user
request, the model parameters or the decoding procedure, and cannot
access gradients or logits. Its goal is a check
$`G_{\mathrm{adv}}(s_{J})`$ on the final state: an unintended tool call,
a disclosure, or a harmful action. When the goal is a tool call, we
assume the targeted tool is in $`\mathcal{T}`$, so that no attack fails
merely because the requested action cannot be executed. We consider
static attacks, where $`\mathrm{adv}`$ is chosen independently of the
defended model, as in InjecAgent, AgentDojo, and AgentDyn.

##### Objectives.

The key quantities of interest are benign utility $`U`$, the proportion
of successful clean episodes (with $`G_{u}(s_{J})=1`$); utility under
attack $`U_{atk}`$, the corresponding proportion on injected episodes;
and attack success rate $`\mathrm{ASR}`$, the proportion of injected
episodes with $`G_{\mathrm{adv}}(s_{J})=1`$. We report the metrics
supported by each benchmark. Let $`\theta_{0}`$ be the parameters of the
base (undefended) model and $`\theta`$ those of the defended one. The
goal is invariance to the injection, i.e. that the defended model on
$`\tilde{c}`$ and the undefended model on $`c`$ induce the same
behavior,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       B_{\theta}(\tilde{c})\ \equiv\ B_{\theta_{0}}(c),
       ```                                                |     | (1) |

where $`B_{\theta}(c)`$ is the distribution over the rest of the episode
induced by the model from context $`c`$, and $`\equiv`$ denotes equality
of the joint distribution of $`(G_{u}(s_{J}),G_{adv}(s_{J}))`$, so that
$`U_{atk}(\theta)=U(\theta_{0})`$ and $`\mathrm{ASR}(\theta)`$ is at the
level the undefended model reaches on the clean context by accident.
[Equation 1](#S3.E1 "In Objectives. ‣ 3.2 Threat Model ‣ 3 Problem Formulation and Threat Model ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
relates two different models on two different contexts: it does not ask
the defended model to ignore tool outputs, only to be insensitive to the
adversarial span that separates $`\tilde{c}`$ from $`c`$. Reporting
$`U`$ and $`U_{atk}`$ next to $`\mathrm{ASR}`$ is essential: a model
that stops calling tools or ends the episode early exposes fewer
opportunities to an attack and reaches a low $`\mathrm{ASR}`$ while
failing.

Figure 2: Output-distribution drift on benign inputs. SFT and DPO shift
the model’s output distribution away from the base model, while
self-distillation keeps it close. Details are in
[Section B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Controlled Output-Distribution Drift Analysis ‣ Appendix B Additional Analysis of Utility Costs ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").

## 4 The Utility Cost of Training-Based Defenses

As discussed earlier, training-based prompt-injection defenses can alter
benign behavior in two ways: by shifting the model’s output distribution
and by leaving tool-use tasks unfinished when completion depends on
guidance from a tool output. We analyze these effects below.

### 4.1 Cost 1: Output-Distribution Drift in Benign Settings

To quantify the first utility cost, we conduct a controlled analysis on
Gemma-4-12B-it using a held-out benign set of 500 standalone questions
drawn from several general-purpose benchmarks. For each question, we
generate the base model’s answer and teacher-force that same answer
through every trained checkpoint. We then compare the next-token
distributions of the base model $`p_{\theta_{0}}`$ and trained model
$`p_{\theta}`$ at each answer position. We report forward and reverse KL
divergence,

[TABLE]

where $`\mathcal{H}`$ contains all evaluated answer prefixes. We also
report top-1 agreement, the fraction of positions where the two models
assign the highest probability to the same next token. The benign-set
construction and full measurement protocol are detailed in
[Section B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Controlled Output-Distribution Drift Analysis ‣ Appendix B Additional Analysis of Utility Costs ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").

To isolate the effect of the objective from that of the data, we
evaluate SFT, DPO, and the self-distillation objective used by RAISED
under the same data and training setup, varying only the objective and
its targets. All methods use 5K injection-augmented trajectories,
rank-16 LoRA, and 313 training steps. Under this short,
parameter-efficient training regime, SFT and DPO induce measurable
output-distribution drift on the held-out benign set. As shown in
[Fig. 2](#S3.F2 "In Objectives. ‣ 3.2 Threat Model ‣ 3 Problem Formulation and Threat Model ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents"),
self-distillation yields forward and reverse KL of only $`0.0010`$,
respectively $`44\times`$ and $`55\times`$ lower than SFT and
$`29\times`$ and $`30\times`$ lower than DPO, while reaching $`0.993`$
top-1 agreement with the base model.
[Section B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Controlled Output-Distribution Drift Analysis ‣ Appendix B Additional Analysis of Utility Costs ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
provides the full controlled setup and shows that the drift increases
with additional SFT and DPO training, while self-distillation remains
close to the base distribution. While this analysis does not establish
that output-distribution drift directly causes downstream utility loss,
it shows that standard defensive training can substantially alter the
model’s behavior on benign inputs, identifying a potential contributor
to utility degradation that self-distillation largely avoids.

### 4.2 Cost 2: Behavioral Drift in Benign Tool Use

Beyond output-distribution drift, defensive training can also change how
the model acts on benign tool outputs.
[Figure 3](#S5.F3 "In 5.1 Stage 1: Self-Generation ‣ 5 Method: RAISED ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
shows a representative example: the base model retrieves a verification
code returned through the available tools and completes the authorized
password change, whereas the defended model stops at that step and asks
the user for the code despite being instructed to complete the task end
to end. This behavior exposes a shortcut in defensive training: the
optimization signal consistently pushes the model away from responses
that follow injected directions in tool outputs, while providing much
less signal for acting on legitimate guidance from the same channel. The
observed failures follow this pattern: the model uses tool outputs as
information while becoming reluctant to act on their guidance, leaving
otherwise solvable tasks unfinished.
[Section B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Behavioral Drift in Benign Tool Use ‣ Appendix B Additional Analysis of Utility Costs ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
provides additional examples across Gemma and Nemotron, including
separate failures for SFT and SecAlign++, and shows that RAISED
completes the corresponding tasks on which these defenses fail.

## 5 Method: RAISED

To address the two forms of utility degradation above, RAISED combines
self-generation and self-distillation as illustrated in Figure 1:
self-generation targets the behavioral failure, while self-distillation
limits output-distribution drift.

### 5.1 Stage 1: Self-Generation

Stage 1 uses the frozen model $`p_{\theta_{0}}`$ in three roles:
generating a scenario, solving and verifying it, and generating an
attack. These roles are executed as independent model calls, with no
model state carried between them.

Scenario generation. The base model generates a small executable
tool-use environment: a world state as a JSON object, tools implemented
as Python functions that read and update it, a user request, and a
Python success check. Each request is designed to require a chain of
dependent tool calls, in which later steps rely on earlier outputs. To
target the failure mode of
[Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Cost 2: Behavioral Drift in Benign Tool Use ‣ 4 The Utility Cost of Training-Based Defenses ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents"),
we steer generation toward scenarios where completing the request
requires acting on legitimate guidance surfaced through a tool output.
For example, the output may reveal a required next step, offer a
recovery path after an unsuccessful action, or indicate that a seemingly
completed step needs follow-up. The trained model must therefore
distinguish such task-relevant guidance from injected instructions. We
create these cases by prompting the model with high-level patterns,
which it may freely instantiate, combine, or extend.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 3: Behavioral drift on a benign tool-use task. The base model
completes the task, while the defended model stops at the tool-guided
step and defers it to the user. This failure pattern occurs in both
prior training-based defenses we study. Additional examples are in
[Section B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Behavioral Drift in Benign Tool Use ‣ Appendix B Additional Analysis of Utility Costs ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").

Solve and verify. The same frozen model then attempts to complete the
user request by interacting with the generated tools. The rollout uses
the model’s standard tool-use interface, without modifying its normal
inference procedure: tool calls are executed against the shared world
state and their actual outputs are returned to the model.

Attack generation. For each retained trajectory, we sample eligible tool
outputs to carry generated injections. For each sampled output, the
frozen model generates the adversarial content and chooses where within
the output to insert it. The attacker is deliberately restricted to the
untrusted channel: it does not observe the user request or the full
task-solving trajectory.

Training data. The retained trajectories, their stored injections, and
the frozen model’s next-token distributions along the model responses
form the training data used in Stage 2.

Details on scenario generation and attack construction are in
[Section C.5.1](#A3.SS5.SSS1 "C.5.1 Self-Generation Details ‣ C.5 RAISED - Robust Attack Invariance through SElf-Distillation ‣ Appendix C Methods Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").

### 5.2 Stage 2: Injection-Augmented Self-Distillation

Stage 2 trains a student model $`p_{\theta}`$, initialized from the same
checkpoint as the frozen model. For each model-generated token position
$`i`$ in a retained trajectory, let $`q_{i}`$ denote the next-token
distribution recorded from the frozen model, and let $`h_{i}`$ denote
the corresponding token history. We construct the student’s input
$`h^{\prime}_{i}`$ as either the original history $`h_{i}`$ or an
injected version $`\tilde{h}_{i}`$, obtained by materializing the stored
injections in their selected tool outputs. The teacher target $`q_{i}`$
is unchanged in both cases.

Let $`\mathcal{I}(\tau)`$ contain the generated token positions in
trajectory $`\tau`$. We train the student by minimizing

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\mathcal{D}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(\tau)}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_{i}\;\middle\|\;p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h^{\prime}_{i})\right),\qquad h^{\prime}_{i}\in\{h_{i},\tilde{h}_{i}\}.
``` |  | (3) |

On clean contexts, the student is trained to remain close to the frozen
model’s original output distribution, limiting the drift identified in
[Section 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Cost 1: Output-Distribution Drift in Benign Settings ‣ 4 The Utility Cost of Training-Based Defenses ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").
On injected examples, the same teacher targets train the student to
recover the original prediction despite the added adversarial content.
Because the legitimate tool content is left unchanged, this encourages
the model to resist the injection while still acting on legitimate
guidance needed to complete the user’s task. The objective therefore
provides a token-level realization of the invariance goal in
[Eq. 1](#S3.E1 "In Objectives. ‣ 3.2 Threat Model ‣ 3 Problem Formulation and Threat Model ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").

For efficiency, we do not store the teacher distribution over the full
vocabulary. At each position $`i`$, we retain the probabilities of the
teacher’s top-$`K`$ tokens and aggregate the remaining probability mass
into a single residual bucket. Let $`\mathcal{V}_{i}^{K}`$ denote the
teacher’s top-$`K`$ tokens. We define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
q_{i}^{\mathrm{rest}}=1-\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{i}^{K}}q_{i}(v),\qquad p_{\theta,i}^{\mathrm{rest}}=1-\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}_{i}^{K}}p_{\theta}(v\mid h^{\prime}_{i}),
``` |  | (4) |

and compute the KL divergence over these $`K+1`$ outcomes. In practice,
the residual bucket generally contains little probability mass on the
order of $`10^{-5}`$. More details are provided in
[Section C.5](#A3.SS5 "C.5 RAISED - Robust Attack Invariance through SElf-Distillation ‣ Appendix C Methods Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").

## 6 Experimental Setup

### 6.1 Models and Evaluated Defenses

##### Models.

Our primary evaluation considers two instruction-tuned, tool-capable
language models from different families: Gemma-4-12B-it and
Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B. Both support structured function calling and
exhibit substantially different baseline susceptibility to indirect
prompt injection. We additionally evaluate RAISED on Qwen3.8-27B in
Appendix [D.6](#A4.SS6 "D.6 Qwen: Additional Low-ASR Stress Test ‣ Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
to test the method in a substantially stronger baseline robustness
regime, where the undefended model already achieves low prompt-injection
attack success rates on AgentDojo and AgentDyn.

##### Evaluated Defenses.

We compare against representative defenses spanning four families.
Vanilla denotes the undefended instruction-tuned model. As
prompting-based defenses, we evaluate Prompt Sandwiching [Learn
Prompting (2024)](#bib.bib31) and Spotlighting [Hines et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib63). As a filtering defense, we use
PromptGuard 2 [Chennabasappa et al. (2025)](#bib.bib62). Finally, among
alignment-based defenses, we evaluate SecAlign++ [Chen et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib10) and RAISED (ours). Trained defenses are run over
three seeds (mean ± std), details are in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Methods Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").

### 6.2 Evaluation Benchmarks

We evaluate defenses along three complementary dimensions. Additional
benchmark and evaluation details are provided in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").

##### Indirect Prompt-Injection Robustness.

We evaluate the security–utility trade-off across three established
benchmarks, measuring benign-task utility ($`U`$), utility under attack
($`U_{\mathrm{atk}}`$), and attack success rate ($`\mathrm{ASR}`$) where
applicable. InjecAgent [Zhan et al. (2024)](#bib.bib49) comprises 1,054
test cases covering Direct Harm and Data Stealing in both Base and
Enhanced settings. AgentDojo [Debenedetti et al. (2024)](#bib.bib14)
covers four environments (workspace, banking, travel, slack) and
evaluates agents under prompt-injection attacks. AgentDyn [Li et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib17) evaluates dynamic, open-ended multi-turn tasks
across Shopping, GitHub, and Daily Life, with injections embedded in
third-party content that may also contain legitimate instructions the
agent must follow.

##### Benign Agentic Capabilities.

To verify that defenses preserve tool-use capabilities in benign
settings, we evaluate across diverse interactive environments:
conversational multi-turn tool use on ToolTalk [Farn and Shin
(2023)](#bib.bib43) and BFCL [Patil et al. (2025)](#bib.bib44); stateful
workplace task completion on WorkBench [Styles et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib45); dynamic multi-mission tool use on Multi-Mission
Tool Bench [Yu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib46); concurrent task execution
under delayed tool responses on AsyncTool [Shi et al.
(2026)](#bib.bib47).

##### General Knowledge and Reasoning.

To verify that training does not degrade general capabilities, we
evaluate all models using the LM Evaluation Harness [Gao et al.
(2021)](#bib.bib32). We assess broad academic knowledge across 57
subjects on MMLU [Hendrycks et al. (2020)](#bib.bib33), challenging
knowledge and reasoning on MMLU-Pro [Wang et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib34),
multilingual knowledge on MMMLU ([OpenAI, 2025](#bib.bib35)),
standardized-exam performance on AGIEval English [Zhong et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib37), and expert-level scientific reasoning on
GPQA-Diamond [Rein et al. (2023)](#bib.bib36). We further evaluate
mathematical reasoning on GSM8K [Cobbe et al. (2021)](#bib.bib39) and
Minerva Math [Lewkowycz et al. (2022)](#bib.bib40), Python code
generation on HumanEval-Instruct [Chen et al. (2021)](#bib.bib41) and
MBPP-Instruct [Odena et al. (2021)](#bib.bib42), and verifiable
instruction following on IFEval [Zhou et al. (2023)](#bib.bib38).

## 7 Results and Analysis

We first evaluate RAISED on Gemma and Nemotron across prompt-injection
robustness, benign agentic and general capabilities.

### 7.1 RAISED improves the security-utility trade-off

attack success together with clean utility ($`U`$) and utility under
attack ($`U_{\mathrm{atk}}`$), since a defense can obtain a low ASR
simply by making the agent less likely to act.

Nemotron shows a complementary pattern: RAISED improves robustness over
SecAlign++, at matched or higher clean utility. AgentDojo ASR falls to
$`0.5\pm 0.1`$% versus $`4.0\pm 0.7`$% for SecAlign++, while AgentDyn
ASR falls to $`1.9\pm 0.6`$% versus $`7.8\pm 0.3`$%. Clean utility
remains close to the Vanilla checkpoint, including 25.0% on AgentDyn.

For SecAlign++, we report the 313-step checkpoint, chosen to avoid
substantial utility degradation. Longer training can further reduce ASR,
but at the cost of broader capability degradation, Appendix
 [D.8](#A4.SS8 "D.8 SecAlign++ training-step trade-off ‣ Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
reports the training-step trade-off.

The filtering baseline further shows why ASR should not be interpreted
in isolation. On Gemma AgentDojo, PromptGuard2 lowers ASR from 39.5% to
16.1%, but $`U_{\mathrm{atk}}`$ falls from 64.0% to 42.9%. RAISED
instead reduces ASR to about 1% while increasing $`U_{\mathrm{atk}}`$ to
$`80.5\pm 0.5`$%.

### 7.2 RAISED preserves benign agentic capabilities

Table [2](#S7.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 7.1 RAISED improves the security-utility trade-off ‣ 7 Results and Analysis ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
reports performance on five benign tool-use benchmarks.

On Gemma, RAISED preserves benign tool-use performance across all five
benchmarks. The largest change is on WorkBench, where performance
increases from 55.9 to $`61.5\pm 0.7`$, while BFCL and MMT-Bench remain
essentially unchanged. A plausible explanation is that RAISED repeatedly
trains on verified multi-step trajectories that require maintaining
state and completing sequences of interdependent actions, which closely
matches the type of task evaluated by WorkBench. Although we do not
isolate this effect causally, the result suggests that robustness
training can reinforce some forms of multi-step tool use rather than
merely preserve them.

Table 3: General capabilities. Results on ten non-agentic benchmarks
covering knowledge, reasoning, multilingual understanding, instruction
following, mathematics, and code generation.

Nemotron shows slightly more variation, but only modest overall changes:
RAISED improves BFCL from 30.0 to $`32.8\pm 0.2`$, remains close to
Vanilla on WorkBench and MMT-Bench, and incurs only moderate decreases
on ToolTalk and AsyncTool.

This contrasts with some inference-time defenses. Prompt Sandwiching,
for example, reduces Gemma BFCL from 57.0 to 33.0 and Nemotron WorkBench
from 21.3 to 12.9, showing that a defense can interfere with legitimate
tool use even without an attack. Across Gemma and Nemotron, we therefore
find no evidence that RAISED achieves low ASR by making the model
generally less agentic: the large security gains coexist with largely
preserved benign tool-use capabilities.

### 7.3 General capabilities remain close to the base model

RAISED preserves general capabilities across all ten benchmarks for
Gemma and Nemotron
(Table [3](#S7.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 7.2 RAISED preserves benign agentic capabilities ‣ 7 Results and Analysis ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")),
with scores close to the Vanilla checkpoints and no systematic
degradation. Variations are small and mixed in sign, indicating that the
gains in prompt-injection robustness do not come at the cost of general
or benign agentic capabilities. This consistency across two model
families supports the objective of clean-context self-distillation,
which constrains defensive training toward behavior already exhibited by
the base model rather than an externally defined target.

We further evaluate RAISED on Qwen3.8-27B, which already exhibits low
prompt-injection ASR, testing whether the defense remains effective in a
stronger robustness regime. RAISED further reduces AgentDojo ASR from
5.8% to $`0.9\pm 0.4`$% and AgentDyn ASR from 4.2% to $`0.1\pm 0.2`$%,
while preserving benign agentic and general capabilities. Full results
are reported in
Appendix [D.6](#A4.SS6 "D.6 Qwen: Additional Low-ASR Stress Test ‣ Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").

### 7.4 Ablation Study

The main comparison preserves SecAlign++’s original fine-tuning data
source, preference-data construction and input representation.
[Appendix E](#A5 "Appendix E Ablation Study ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
instead controls the training data and inputs while varying the
objective, and then fixes the objective while varying the data source.
The results show that self-distillation preserves more agentic utility
than SFT and SecAlign++’s DPO objective at similar robustness, while our
self-generated trajectories provide a further gain in utility.

## 8 Conclusion

We introduced RAISED, a self-distillation defense that trains the model
to be invariant to prompt injection. The model generates its own
tool-use scenarios and injections, including cases where completing the
task requires acting on legitimate guidance from a tool output, and
learns to match its clean-context next-token distributions on injected
contexts. RAISED matches or exceeds the robustness of SecAlign++ while
better preserving benign utility, and induces far less distribution
drift than SFT or DPO. More broadly, when the desired behavior already
exists in the clean model, defensive training should preserve it under
attack rather than learn a new defensive policy. Since RAISED preserves
the base model’s behavior rather than improving it, it also inherits its
errors; we discuss this and other limitations in
[Appendix G](#A7 "Appendix G Limitations ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents"),
and broader impact in
[Appendix H](#A8 "Appendix H Broader Impact ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").

### AI use statement

Generative AI tools were used during the preparation of this manuscript
for stylistic editing and language refinement, for assistance in
debugging code, and to help identify potentially relevant literature.
They were not used to generate the scientific ideas, methodology,
experimental design, figures, or results presented in this work. All
AI-assisted revisions were reviewed by the authors, debugging
suggestions were manually verified, and every cited reference was
independently checked and incorporated by the authors from the original
source. The authors take full responsibility for the final content of
the manuscript.

### Ethics statement

This work studies defenses against indirect prompt injection in
tool-using language-model agents. Because the evaluation and training
procedures include the generation and execution of adversarial prompt
injections, the techniques described in this paper have potential
dual-use implications. Our intent is to improve the robustness and
reliability of language-model agents operating over untrusted external
content. The attacks considered in this work are evaluated in controlled
benchmark environments and are used to measure and strengthen defensive
behavior. RAISED should be viewed as a defense-in-depth mechanism and
not as a substitute for established safeguards such as access control,
sandboxing, capability restriction, and least-privilege tool design.

### Reproducibility statement

We provide the information required to reproduce our method and
experiments throughout the paper and appendices. The RAISED training
procedure is specified in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Method: RAISED ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents"),
including the self-generation and injection-augmented self-distillation
objectives.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Methods Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
provides the implementation details, training configurations,
optimization settings, dataset construction procedure, and compute
setup.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
describes the evaluation protocols, benchmark-specific metrics, and
experimental settings used for the reported results. Additional
analyses, including the controlled distribution-drift study and
behavioral failure cases, are documented in the corresponding appendix
sections. An anonymous Git repository containing the source code,
training scripts, evaluation pipelines, and experiment configurations
used in this work is provided with the supplementary material. Code
available at
[https://github.com/orailix/RAISED](https://github.com/orailix/RAISED)
