````math
## Appendix A Formal Setting and Notation

##### Scenario.

A scenario is $`(\mathcal{S},s_{0},\mathcal{T},u,G_{u})`$: a state space
with initial state $`s_{0}`$, a tool menu $`\mathcal{T}`$, a user
request $`u`$, and a success predicate $`G_{u}:\mathcal{S}\to\{0,1\}`$.
A tool $`t\in\mathcal{T}`$ is shown to the model as a name, a
description, and an argument schema $`\mathcal{A}_{t}`$, and is executed
by
$`f_{t}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}_{t}\to\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{O}`$,
which updates the state and returns an observation. In self-generated
scenarios
([Section 5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Stage 1: Self-Generation ‣ 5 Method: RAISED ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")),
$`s_{0}`$ is a JSON object, $`f_{t}`$ a deterministic Python function,
and $`G_{u}`$ a Python predicate on the final state or on the final
answer.

##### Episode.

At turn $`j`$ the agent emits $`a_{j}`$, either a tool call
$`(t_{j},\alpha_{j})`$, after which
$`(s_{j},o_{j})=f_{t_{j}}(s_{j-1},\alpha_{j})`$, or a final answer. The
context before turn $`j`$ is
$`c_{j}=\rho(\sigma,\mathcal{T},u,a_{1},o_{1},\dots,a_{j-1},o_{j-1})`$,
with $`\sigma`$ the system prompt and $`\rho`$ the chat template; each
token carries a provenance label in
$`\{\textsc{sys},\textsc{user},\textsc{asst},\textsc{tool}\}`$. Actions
are sampled token by token from the policy
$`\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid c_{j})`$ induced by $`p_{\theta}`$. The
trajectory $`\tau=(a_{1},o_{1},\dots,a_{J})`$ succeeds if
$`G_{u}(s_{J})=1`$.

##### Injection.

The adversary picks a string $`\mathrm{adv}`$, a turn $`j`$, and an
offset $`k`$, and the environment returns
$`o_{j}[:k]\,\|\,\mathrm{adv}\,\|\,o_{j}[k:]`$ in place of $`o_{j}`$.
The injected context $`\tilde{c}`$ differs from $`c`$ only on
tool-labelled spans. Distractor tools $`\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{adv}}`$
needed by the attacker goal $`G_{\mathrm{adv}}`$ are added to
$`\mathcal{T}`$ on both sides.

##### Metrics.

$`B_{\theta}(c)`$ is the distribution over the rest of the episode
induced by $`\pi_{\theta}`$ and $`\{f_{t}\}`$ from $`c`$. Over the
scenarios of a benchmark, $`U(\theta)=\Pr[G_{u}(s_{J})=1]`$ on clean
episodes, and $`U_{\mathrm{atk}}(\theta)=\Pr[G_{u}(s_{J})=1]`$,
$`\mathrm{ASR}(\theta)=\Pr[G_{\mathrm{adv}}(s_{J})=1]`$ on injected
ones. $`B_{\theta}(\tilde{c})\equiv B_{\theta_{0}}(c)`$ in
[Eq. 1](#S3.E1 "In Objectives. ‣ 3.2 Threat Model ‣ 3 Problem Formulation and Threat Model ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
means equality of the joint distribution of
$`(G_{u}(s_{J}),G_{\mathrm{adv}}(s_{J}))`$. Benchmark-specific
predicates are in
[Section D.5](#A4.SS5 "D.5 Agentic Prompt-Injection Evaluation ‣ Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").

| Symbol | Meaning |
|----|----|
| $`\mathcal{S}`$, $`s_{0}`$, $`s_{J}`$ | State space; initial and final state of an episode |
| $`\mathcal{T}`$, $`\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{adv}}`$ | Tool menu; distractor tools added for the attacker goal |
| $`\mathcal{A}_{t}`$, $`f_{t}`$ | Argument space and executor of tool $`t`$ |
| $`o_{j}`$, $`a_{j}`$ | $`j`$-th tool observation (untrusted); $`j`$-th assistant action |
| $`\sigma`$, $`u`$ | System prompt; user request |
| $`\rho`$ | Chat template |
| $`c`$, $`\tilde{c}`$ | Clean context; injected context |
| $`\tau`$ | Trajectory $`(a_{1},o_{1},\dots,a_{J})`$ |
| $`\pi_{\theta}`$, $`B_{\theta}(c)`$ | Policy induced by $`p_{\theta}`$; behavior (distribution over the rest of the episode) |
| $`G_{u}`$, $`G_{\mathrm{adv}}`$ | Task-success and attacker-goal predicates on the final state |
| $`\mathrm{adv}`$ | Injected string |
| $`\mathcal{D}`$ | Training distribution over retained trajectories |
| $`\mathcal{I}(\tau)`$ | Supervised positions in trajectory $`\tau`$ (model-generated tokens) |
| $`K`$ | Number of stored teacher tokens per position ($`K=256`$) |
| $`U`$, $`U_{\mathrm{atk}}`$, $`\mathrm{ASR}`$ | Benign utility; utility under attack; attack success rate |

Table 4: Notation.

## Appendix B Additional Analysis of Utility Costs

### B.1 Controlled Output-Distribution Drift Analysis

##### Controlled training setup.

We compare SFT, DPO, and self-distillation while holding the training
data and parameter-efficient fine-tuning setup fixed. All three
objectives use the same 5K injection-augmented tool-use trajectories,
with identical trajectory contexts, injection placements, and supervised
model-generated positions, and are trained with rank-16 LoRA for 313
steps. They differ only in their supervision: SFT uses fixed response
targets, DPO contrasts preferred and rejected responses generated from
the frozen base model, and self-distillation uses the frozen base
model’s next-token distribution.

##### Benign evaluation set.

We construct a held-out set of 500 standalone questions, with 125
examples from each of four public benchmark sources: ARC-Easy, TriviaQA,
GSM8K, and SciQ. These questions contain neither tool use nor prompt
injections and are used only for this analysis. We retain questions that
the base model answers correctly, so the comparison focuses on behavior
already exhibited by the original checkpoint. We also remove any
question liable to provoke a refusal or guarded reply.

##### Measurement protocol.

For each question, we first generate the base model’s greedy answer
$`y_{1:T}`$. We then teacher-force that same answer through the base
model and every trained checkpoint and record the next-token
distribution $`p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})`$ at each answer position
$`t`$. Forward and reverse KL divergence are averaged over all evaluated
positions and questions, as defined in
[Eq. 2](#S4.E2 "In 4.1 Cost 1: Output-Distribution Drift in Benign Settings ‣ 4 The Utility Cost of Training-Based Defenses ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").
We also report top-1 agreement, the fraction of positions at which the
trained checkpoint and base model assign highest probability to the same
next token. Using the same answer prefixes for every checkpoint isolates
changes in the predictive distributions from differences caused by
generating different answers.

##### Source of distribution drift.

The three objectives differ in how they constrain the trained model
relative to the base model. SFT maximizes the likelihood of a fixed
target sequence. At each supervised position, this pushes probability
toward the target token but does not preserve the base model’s
probabilities over alternative tokens; when the targets come from
another source, the resulting distribution can therefore move away from
the base model.

DPO is also not a direct distribution-matching objective. For a
preference example $`(x,y_{w},y_{l})`$, its loss can be written as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}=-\log\sigma\!\left(\beta\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{w}\mid x)}{\pi_{0}(y_{w}\mid x)}-\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{l}\mid x)}{\pi_{0}(y_{l}\mid x)}\right]\right),
``` |  | (5) |

where $`\pi_{0}`$ is the frozen reference model. Although DPO is derived
from a KL-regularized preference-learning objective [Rafailov et al.
(2024)](#bib.bib30), the training loss above constrains the relative
preference between two sequences rather than directly matching the
model’s next-token distribution to that of the reference model.

This distinction is particularly relevant for SecAlign-style
prompt-injection training. In SecAlign, both responses are optimized
under a context containing an injection. SecAlign++ improves target
construction by generating the preferred response from the base model on
the corresponding clean input, but DPO still evaluates the preferred and
rejected responses under the injected training context [Chen et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib4); [Chen et al. (2026)](#bib.bib10). Thus, the base
model’s predictive distribution on the clean context is not directly
used as a training constraint.

A local analysis illustrates why improving the DPO preference margin
does not necessarily preserve even the preferred response likelihood.
Let

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
g_{w}=\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{w}\mid x),\qquad g_{l}=\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{l}\mid x).
``` |  |

For a gradient-descent step on a single preference pair, the update has
the form

|     |                                                  |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Delta\theta=\alpha(g_{w}-g_{l}),\qquad\alpha>0,
       ```                                               |     |

where $`\alpha`$ absorbs the learning rate and the positive scalar
factor from the DPO loss. To first order,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{w}\mid x)`$ | $`\displaystyle\approx\alpha\left(\lVert g_{w}\rVert^{2}-g_{w}^{\top}g_{l}\right),`$ |  | (6) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\Delta\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{l}\mid x)`$ | $`\displaystyle\approx\alpha\left(g_{w}^{\top}g_{l}-\lVert g_{l}\rVert^{2}\right).`$ |  | (7) |

At the same time, the preference margin changes by

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta\!\left[\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{w}\mid x)-\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{l}\mid x)\right]\approx\alpha\lVert g_{w}-g_{l}\rVert^{2}\geq 0.
``` |  |

Since the reference model is fixed, this is also the change in the
log-ratio margin optimized by DPO. Nevertheless, both likelihoods
decrease whenever

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\lVert g_{w}\rVert^{2}<g_{w}^{\top}g_{l}<\lVert g_{l}\rVert^{2}.
``` |  | (8) |

Thus, increasing the DPO preference margin does not imply preserving the
likelihood of the preferred response. Decreases in preferred-response
likelihood under preference optimization have been studied previously as
likelihood displacement [Razin et al. (2025)](#bib.bib64). That work
studies the phenomenon in general preference-learning and
safety-alignment settings, rather than prompt-injection defenses or
tool-use agents. Here, we use the same mechanism only to explain why a
SecAlign-style preference objective need not preserve the base model’s
behavior in benign settings; our controlled experiment directly measures
this drift in the prompt-injection setting.

RAISED instead directly matches the base model’s predictive distribution
on the clean context. On clean examples this anchors the student to the
original distribution, while on injected examples the same target
teaches the student to recover that distribution despite the added
injection. The top-$`K`$ plus residual approximation described in
[Eq. 4](#S5.E4 "In 5.2 Stage 2: Injection-Augmented Self-Distillation ‣ 5 Method: RAISED ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
makes this distributional constraint practical.

##### Longer-training drift.

Under the longer 10K-example training schedule, SFT and DPO drift
further from the base model. SFT reaches forward and reverse KL
divergences of 0.0609 and 0.0773, respectively, compared with 0.044 and
0.055 under the 5K schedule, while DPO increases from 0.029 and 0.030 to
0.0370 and 0.0402. Self-distillation remains substantially closer to the
base distribution, with forward and reverse KL divergences of only
0.0016 and 0.0017. Thus, additional training amplifies the
distributional drift induced by SFT and DPO, while self-distillation
maintains much lower drift.

### B.2 Behavioral Drift in Benign Tool Use

##### Setup.

We illustrate the behavioral failure mode of
[Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Cost 2: Behavioral Drift in Benign Tool Use ‣ 4 The Utility Cost of Training-Based Defenses ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
on benign, injection-free tool-use tasks. In every example, the base
model completes the user’s request, while at least one training-based
defense leaves it unfinished despite having access to the tools needed
to complete the authorized task. The examples focus on cases where
completing the request requires acting on guidance supplied through a
tool output.

##### Scope of the evidence.

These examples are intended to characterize the failure mode rather than
estimate its prevalence. We include a broad set of standard agentic
benchmarks to support comparable evaluation of benign tool-use utility
across defenses, but those benchmarks are not constructed to isolate
this particular behavior. The interaction pattern itself is important in
realistic tool use: a tool output may surface a verification
requirement, corrected retry target, prerequisite, or follow-up action
that is necessary to complete the user’s authorized task. AgentDojo
contains such cases, and AgentDyn more directly includes helpful
third-party guidance that the agent may need to act on. Our examples
show that training-based defenses can fail on this class of interaction,
but they do not establish how frequently such cases arise in deployed
systems. Estimating their real-world prevalence would require deployment
data beyond the scope of our evaluation. Nevertheless, these
interactions represent plausible and operationally important workflows,
since failing to act on the returned guidance can leave an authorized
task incomplete. A broader quantitative evaluation of both the
prevalence of these cases and defense behavior on them remains important
future work.

##### Gemma examples.

[Table 5](#A2.T5 "In Gemma examples. ‣ B.2 Behavioral Drift in Benign Tool Use ‣ Appendix B Additional Analysis of Utility Costs ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
combines four examples from AgentDojo and AgentDyn with three additional
designed cases. Among the benchmark examples, SecAlign++ leaves two
tasks unfinished and completes two; among the designed cases, it leaves
two unfinished and completes one. SFT leaves all seven unfinished, while
the base model and RAISED complete every task.

|  Task |  Base |  SFT |  SecAlign++ |  RAISED |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  Change the account password; a tool emails a verification code |  reads code, updates ✓ |  claims completion without reading code $`\times`$ |  asks user for code $`\times`$ |  reads code, updates ✓ |
|  Follow instructions in a file; the file says to adjust a standing order |  updates standing order ✓ |  relays instruction, no update $`\times`$ |  updates standing order ✓ |  updates standing order ✓ |
|  Transfer the most-starred repository to an address read from the inbox |  transfers and verifies ✓ |  claims completion without verification $`\times`$ |  transfers and verifies ✓ |  transfers and verifies ✓ |
|  Invite the collaborator who requested it; a tool emails a verification code |  reads code, invites ✓ |  claims sent without verification $`\times`$ |  claims sent without verification $`\times`$ |  reads code, invites ✓ |
|  Release the batch; an error identifies the corrected record to release |  releases corrected record ✓ |  claims completion, releases nothing $`\times`$ |  asks user whether to release it $`\times`$ |  releases corrected record ✓ |
|  Open the course for enrollment; the tool says to publish the syllabus first |  publishes, then opens ✓ |  asks user to publish first $`\times`$ |  asks whether to publish first $`\times`$ |  publishes, then opens ✓ |
|  Import the reservations; the endpoint says to retry with an updated dialect |  retries and imports ✓ |  tells user to retry $`\times`$ |  retries and imports ✓ |  retries and imports ✓ |

Table 5: Behavioral drift on benign Gemma tool-use tasks. The first four
rows are examples from AgentDojo and AgentDyn; the final three are
designed cases covering additional forms of tool-supplied guidance. A ✓
indicates task completion and $`\times`$ a failure to complete the
required authorized steps.

##### Nemotron examples.

We observe the same pattern on Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B using four
designed benign tasks in
[Table 6](#A2.T6 "In Nemotron examples. ‣ B.2 Behavioral Drift in Benign Tool Use ‣ Appendix B Additional Analysis of Utility Costs ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").
SecAlign++ leaves two of the four unfinished and completes the other
two, while SFT leaves all four unfinished. The base model and RAISED
complete every task. The two SecAlign++ failures are observed across
three seeds and repeated runs.

|  Task |  Base |  SFT |  SecAlign++ |  RAISED |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  Publish the menu; an error returns the corrected versioned target |  publishes corrected target ✓ |  claims completion, wrong target $`\times`$ |  publishes original target $`\times`$ |  publishes corrected target ✓ |
|  Post the store-opening summary; the required post step is named only in a tool output |  posts summary ✓ |  lists statuses, does not post $`\times`$ |  describes summary, does not post $`\times`$ |  posts summary ✓ |
|  Sync the inventory; the service says to retry with an updated version |  retries and syncs ✓ |  tells user to retry $`\times`$ |  retries and syncs ✓ |  retries and syncs ✓ |
|  Finalize payroll; the tool says timesheets must be validated first |  validates, then finalizes ✓ |  claims completion, skips validation $`\times`$ |  validates, then finalizes ✓ |  validates, then finalizes ✓ |

Table 6: Behavioral drift on designed benign Nemotron tool-use tasks.
Each task requires acting on guidance returned by a first-party tool.

Across both models, the failures have the same basic form: the defended
model obtains the relevant information from the tool output but does not
reliably act on it when a subsequent authorized step is required. The
SecAlign++ success cases also show that the effect is not universal
across all forms of tool-supplied guidance. RAISED preserves the
corresponding base-model behavior throughout.

## Appendix C Methods Details

### C.1 Prompt Sandwiching

Prompt sandwiching, also called the *repeat-user-prompt* defense, is a
training-free defense that restates the user’s task after untrusted
content [Learn Prompting (2024)](#bib.bib31). Following the
implementation from SecAlign++ [Chen et al. (2026)](#bib.bib10), we
append the reminder “Please always remember that your task is: \<task\>”
after every new tool response and assign it the user role. For
multi-turn interactions, the same original task is repeated after each
successive tool response. As illustrated in
Figure [4](#A3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ C.1 Prompt Sandwiching ‣ Appendix C Methods Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents"),
this places the trusted task immediately before the model’s next
generation. Prompt sandwiching requires no fine-tuning or auxiliary
model, but increases the context length by repeating the task after
every tool response.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 4: Message feed before and after prompt sandwiching.

### C.2 Spotlighting

Spotlighting is a family of prompt-engineering defenses that transforms
untrusted text to help the model distinguish it from trusted
instructions [Hines et al. (2024)](#bib.bib63). We use its delimiting
variant, following the spotlighting_with_delimiting implementation
evaluated in AgentDojo [Debenedetti et al. (2024)](#bib.bib14). We
append an instruction to the system prompt explaining that tool outputs
will appear between \<\< and \>\> and that instructions within these
delimiters must not be followed. Every tool response is then wrapped
with these markers, as illustrated in
Figure [5](#A3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ C.2 Spotlighting ‣ Appendix C Methods Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").
The transformation is applied independently to each new tool response
and requires no fine-tuning or auxiliary model.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 5: Message feed before and after spotlighting with delimiting.

### C.3 PromptGuard2

Prompt Guard 2 is an 86M-parameter classifier developed by Meta to
detect prompt injections and jailbreaks [Chennabasappa et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib62). Following the implementation from AgentDyn [Li et
al. (2026)](#bib.bib17), we apply the classifier independently to every
new tool response and classify it as an injection when its safety score
is below $`0.5`$. Responses classified as safe are left unchanged, while
flagged responses are replaced in full by “\<Data omitted because a
prompt injection was detected\>” before being passed to the agent, as
illustrated in
Figure [6](#A3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ C.3 PromptGuard2 ‣ Appendix C Methods Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").
Unlike the previous prompting defenses, this method removes suspicious
content from the model’s context but requires running an auxiliary
classifier after each tool call.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 6: Message feed before and after filtering a tool response with
Prompt Guard 2.

### C.4 SecAlign++

SecAlign++ ([Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib10)) is the closest
training-based baseline to RAISED. It refines SecAlign ([Chen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4)) with three changes. First, the chat template gains a
dedicated role for untrusted content, so that the model can learn to
follow instructions from the system and user roles while treating text
in that role as data. Second, training-time injections are placed before
or after the clean input at random, rather than always appended to it,
which prevents the model from learning a positional shortcut. Third, the
preferred response in each preference pair is the undefended model’s own
response to the clean instruction alone, so that the target is
in-distribution for the model being trained, whereas the rejected
response is the undefended model’s own response to the injected
instruction alone, both sampled independently rather than produced
within a single shared context. The model is then trained with DPO on
these pairs, using LoRA.

##### Adaptation to tool use.

The original recipe targets single-turn instruction following, with the
untrusted content held in a single input message. We adapt it to the
agentic setting at inference time by rendering tool-response messages
with the input role of the SecAlign template, so that the model applies
the learned trust boundary to real tool output.

The preference data follow the original SecAlign++ recipe: pairs are
constructed from the Cleaned-Alpaca instruction set ([Ruebsamen,
2023](#bib.bib65)), and therefore contain no tool calls or tool
responses. SecAlign++ is nevertheless evaluated by its authors on
AgentDojo and other agentic benchmarks, relying on the learned trust
boundary to transfer from single-turn untrusted inputs to tool outputs.
We preserve this training setup for the method-level comparison. Our
ablation in
[Appendix E](#A5 "Appendix E Ablation Study ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
separately evaluates the SecAlign++ DPO objective on agentic
trajectories while controlling the training data and input
representation.

##### Hyperparameters.

We fine-tune with DPO ($`\beta=0.1`$) and LoRA (rank 16, $`\alpha=32`$,
applied to the query, key, value and output projections) for one epoch
over 5,008 examples subsampled from Cleaned-Alpaca (313 steps at batch
size 16), with a constant learning rate of $`2\times 10^{-5}`$ and no
warm-up, in bfloat16 on one GB200 GPU per run; training is repeated over
three seeds. This is a considerably smaller budget than the original
recipe, which trains for several epochs over the full 51K-example set,
and matches the budget of the controlled comparison in
[Section 4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Cost 1: Output-Distribution Drift in Benign Settings ‣ 4 The Utility Cost of Training-Based Defenses ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents");
the 625-step checkpoint of
[Section D.8](#A4.SS8 "D.8 SecAlign++ training-step trade-off ‣ Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
uses the same 10K-example training budget as RAISED. We use the 313-step
checkpoint in the main comparison as a common operating point on the
robustness–utility trade-off. On Gemma, SecAlign++ already reaches
near-zero ASR on InjecAgent and AgentDojo at this budget and further
training primarily reduces utility without materially improving
robustness. On Nemotron, extending training to 625 steps further reduces
ASR on AgentDojo and AgentDyn, but also increases degradation on several
general and agentic capability benchmarks; the same qualitative
trade-off is observed for Gemma and Qwen
([Section D.8](#A4.SS8 "D.8 SecAlign++ training-step trade-off ‣ Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")).
We therefore report the longer-training results separately.

### C.5 RAISED - Robust Attack Invariance through SElf-Distillation

#### C.5.1 Self-Generation Details

##### Overview.

Self-generation uses independent calls to the same frozen checkpoint
$`p_{\theta_{0}}`$ for scenario generation, task solving, and attack
generation; no model state is carried between these calls. The scenario
generator first creates an executable tool-use task. A separate call to
the frozen model then solves and validates the task through its standard
tool-use interface, after which additional calls generate prompt
injections for selected tool outputs. Each model family generates and
solves its own scenarios using the same generation procedure. Generation
continues until 10,000 validated trajectories are retained for each
model.

##### Executable scenario generation.

The scenario generator produces a world state represented as JSON, a
user request, an executable success check, and a menu of 3–6 tools. Each
tool has a model-visible name, description, and argument schema,
together with a deterministic Python implementation that reads or
updates the shared world state. The implementation is executed in a
sandbox and is never exposed to the agent. Generated tools and schemas
are validated before rollout to ensure that they can be executed
consistently.

The user request specifies an end goal rather than an explicit sequence
of tool calls. The generator is prompted toward tasks requiring several
dependent calls, typically 3–8, so that information obtained earlier in
the trajectory is needed to make progress later. Tool menus similarly
contain complementary capabilities rather than multiple near-duplicate
operations.

##### Failure-focused structures.

A central goal of self-generation is to increase the number of benign
tasks in which legitimate guidance returned through a tool must
determine what the agent does next. We therefore guide generation toward
three high-level structures that directly target the behavioral drift
identified in
[Section 4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Cost 2: Behavioral Drift in Benign Tool Use ‣ 4 The Utility Cost of Training-Based Defenses ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").
These structures specify the dependency that should be present while
leaving the domain, tools, entities, records, and concrete interaction
to the generating model.

|  Structure |  Construction |
|----|----|
|  Surfaced guidance |  A step required to complete the user’s task is revealed through a tool output rather than stated in the original request. The output may directly indicate the next operation or identify the resource, record, or location needed to determine it. |
|  Recovery / completion |  An intermediate observation reveals how an incomplete task can be continued, for example by exposing a supported alternative after an unsuccessful action, identifying another resource needed for completion, or showing that another user-requested obligation remains. |
|  Follow-through |  An action that appears to complete the request instead returns a provisional or incomplete result, requiring one or more additional authorized actions before the task is actually finished. |

Table 7: Failure-focused structures used during self-generation. Each
structure creates a benign task in which information returned through a
tool must legitimately influence a subsequent authorized action.

In surfaced-guidance scenarios, the required step is intentionally
absent from the original user request and becomes apparent only after
interacting with a tool. The tool output may explicitly specify the next
operation, provide the information needed to perform it, or point to
another resource from which that information must be obtained. The
generated success check requires the resulting step to be completed.

For a subset of these scenarios, the legitimate guidance is deliberately
expressed in a surface form resembling the kinds of directives that can
appear in prompt injections. It may resemble a workflow instruction,
correction, status message, or authoritative notice while remaining
necessary for the user’s original task. These examples make surface form
alone insufficient to determine whether guidance from a tool output
should be acted on.

Recovery/completion scenarios introduce the information needed to
continue an otherwise incomplete trajectory through an intermediate
observation. An unsuccessful action may reveal a supported alternative
or corrected target; an intermediate artifact may point to another
resource needed for completion; or an apparently satisfied subgoal may
leave another part of the user’s request unresolved. Follow-through
scenarios instead make an apparently terminal operation return a
pending, provisional, partial, or otherwise incomplete result, requiring
the model to continue beyond the first apparent success.

##### Broader tool-use coverage.

Alongside the failure-focused structures, we sample additional
structural requirements whose purpose is to broaden the kinds of benign
tool use represented in the corpus. When selected, each requirement is
added to the scenario-generation prompt as a high-level constraint;
compatible requirements may occur together, while the generating model
chooses the concrete domain, tools, entities, and interaction that
realize them.

Read-and-report scenarios are requested to be read-only tasks whose
answer depends on several dependent tool calls rather than a single
lookup, for example by requiring information to be retrieved, combined,
compared, or aggregated across multiple outputs. Clarification scenarios
are constructed so that one user-specific value required for completion
is absent from the request and cannot be recovered from the world state
or available tools. The model must therefore make any progress that is
possible and ask the user for the missing value; once it is supplied,
the same task continues to completion.

Derived-value scenarios require a later answer or tool argument to be
computed from quantities returned by earlier tools rather than copied
directly from an observation. For action tasks, the computed value must
be used in a subsequent tool call; for read-only tasks, it must appear
in the final answer. The expected value is recomputed independently
during verification. Eligible scenarios can additionally span multiple
interaction turns with a changing tool menu: an initial set of tools
supports discovery or preparation, after which an additional capability
becomes available while preserving the same world state and user goal.

##### Sampling and structural coverage.

The structural requirements are sampled before scenario generation and
determine which high-level constraints are included in the generation
prompt. Compatible requirements can be active in the same scenario.
Their sampling probabilities therefore control how often a structure is
requested, not how often it appears in the final training corpus: after
generation, the scenario must still be solved successfully and pass the
common execution-based and structure-specific verification pipeline.

Different structures survive this pipeline at different rates. To
calibrate the sampling probabilities, for each structure and each model
family we run 50 pilot generations with that structure activated while
the other compatible structures follow their normal sampling procedure,
and measure the fraction ultimately retained after solving and
verification. We use these empirical keep rates to choose one set of
sampling probabilities, shared across model families, that gives the
active structures a reasonably balanced presence in the retained
corpora.

Surfaced guidance and recovery/completion are sampled with probability
$`0.40`$, follow-through with $`0.35`$, read-and-report and
clarification with $`0.25`$ each, and derived-value tasks with $`0.15`$.
The changing-tool-menu structure is applied whenever an eligible
scenario is generated. Within surfaced-guidance cases, injection-like
surface phrasing is sampled with probability $`0.30`$.

##### Diversity across generated scenarios.

The structural requirements specify properties of the interaction rather
than complete task templates. To vary their concrete realization, the
scenario-generation prompt is additionally varied along several
dimensions independently of the selected structures. We sample cues for
the application domain, concrete entities and attributes, tool
capabilities, and the dependency shape connecting successive operations.
These cues guide generation but do not fix the resulting task: the model
may replace, combine, or extend them while satisfying the requested
structural constraints.

As a result, the same high-level structure can be instantiated with
different domains, records and entities, tool menus, and patterns of
dependency between calls. For example, the dependency cues can induce
sequential retrieval, information gathered from multiple sources,
transformations of intermediate values, or verify-then-act workflows
without tying any of these forms to a particular application domain.
Scenario generation uses temperature $`0.9`$.

##### Solve and validate.

A separate call to the same frozen model receives the generated user
request and model-visible tool schemas and attempts to complete the task
through its standard tool-use interface using greedy decoding. Each
emitted tool call is executed against the shared world state, its actual
output is returned to the model, and state mutations persist across
subsequent calls. The rollout continues until the model produces a final
answer or reaches the execution limit.

Generated scenarios are filtered before entering the training corpus.
Tool implementations and schemas must be executable and internally
consistent, and the resulting trajectory must satisfy its generated
success criterion. For state-changing tasks, the success check evaluates
the resulting world state and is required to fail on the initial state
and pass on the final state, preventing already-satisfied tasks from
being retained. For read-only tasks, completion is instead verified from
the model’s final answer. Scenarios that cannot be executed consistently
or remain incomplete after rollout are discarded. Structure-specific
checks additionally verify that the dependency requested during
generation is actually realized in the resulting task.

##### Attack generation.

Attack generation is performed only after a clean trajectory has been
successfully solved and verified. For each retained scenario, a separate
generation step produces a concrete adversarial objective appropriate to
the scenario and, when needed, plausible in-domain attacker tools that
make the objective executable. Any attacker tools are included in both
the clean and injected contexts, so their presence alone does not
distinguish the injected example.

Injection points are sampled from tool-output occurrences that actually
appear in the verified trajectory. For each selected output, the
injection writer receives the clean tool output, the adversarial
objective, the available tool schemas, any attacker tools, and any
injections already placed earlier in the same trajectory. It does not
receive the user request, the complete solution, or the full
task-solving trajectory. The writer generates the adversarial text and
chooses its placement within the selected output, either embedding it in
an existing string field or placing it before or after the original
content. The requested placement is validated against the actual output
and stored so that the same transformation can be reconstructed during
training.

Attack wording is varied independently of the benign scenario across
human-like, system- or workflow-like, and more open-ended forms. When
multiple injections are generated for the same trajectory, later
generations are encouraged to differ from earlier ones. Attack
generation uses temperature $`0.9`$.

##### Teacher targets and training data.

Each retained example stores the verified clean trajectory together with
its injection specifications. During training, the stored injections are
materialized in their selected tool outputs, leaving the remainder of
the trajectory unchanged. The teacher target is always obtained from the
frozen model on the corresponding clean trajectory.

At each supervised model-generated token position, we retain the
teacher’s top-$`K`$ next-token probabilities with $`K=256`$ and
aggregate the remaining probability mass into the residual bucket
defined in
[Eq. 4](#S5.E4 "In 5.2 Stage 2: Injection-Augmented Self-Distillation ‣ 5 Method: RAISED ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").
For each model, the final self-generated training corpus contains 10,000
retained trajectories.

##### Training configuration.

The student is initialized from the same checkpoint as the frozen
generator and teacher. We train it with LoRA applied to all linear
layers, using a learning rate of $`5\times 10^{-5}`$ and batch size
$`16`$ for one epoch on the $`10,000`$ generated cases, with an
injection ratio of 0.5. Training uses the injection-augmented
self-distillation objective described in
[Section 5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Stage 2: Injection-Augmented Self-Distillation ‣ 5 Method: RAISED ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").

## Appendix D Evaluation Details

### D.1 Evaluation Protocol

We evaluate SecAlign++ and RAISED over three training seeds and report
the mean and standard deviation across seeds. All other methods are
evaluated once because they do not involve a stochastic training run.

### D.2 Architectural diversity.

We deliberately selected models with substantially different
architectures to test whether RAISED depends on a particular transformer
design. Gemma-4-12B-it uses a dense architecture combining
sliding-window and full-attention layers, whereas
Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B uses a hybrid architecture that combines
attention, Mamba-style state-space layers, and mixture-of-experts (MoE)
blocks. Qwen3.8-27B provides a third configuration, interleaving
linear-attention and full-attention layers. This diversity allows us to
evaluate whether the proposed self-distillation objective transfers
across different sequence-modeling mechanisms and parameter-routing
strategies, rather than being specific to a single model architecture.

### D.3 General-Knowledge Evaluation

We evaluate general knowledge and related capabilities to measure
whether the defense methods preserve broad knowledge and general
problem-solving capabilities.

##### LM Evaluation Harness.

We use the LM Evaluation Harness [Gao et al. (2021)](#bib.bib32) for all
reported general-knowledge evaluations. For each benchmark, we report
the group-level metric produced by LM Evaluation Harness. Group metrics
are micro-averaged over evaluation samples, such that every question,
prompt, or programming problem receives equal weight.

##### MMLU.

MMLU [Hendrycks et al. (2020)](#bib.bib33) evaluates broad knowledge and
reasoning through multiple-choice questions spanning 57 subjects across
the humanities, social sciences, STEM, and professional domains. We
report accuracy, where a response is correct when the answer option
assigned the highest likelihood matches the reference option.

##### MMLU-Pro.

MMLU-Pro [Wang et al. (2024b)](#bib.bib34) evaluates more challenging,
reasoning-intensive multiple-choice questions organized into broad
subject categories. We report exact-match accuracy after applying the
benchmark’s answer-extraction procedure to the generated response.

##### Multilingual MMLU.

Multilingual MMLU ([OpenAI, 2025](#bib.bib35)) evaluates knowledge and
reasoning across multiple languages and subject areas using multilingual
versions of MMLU-style multiple-choice questions. We report accuracy,
where a response is correct when the answer option assigned the highest
likelihood matches the reference option.

##### GPQA Diamond.

GPQA Diamond [Rein et al. (2023)](#bib.bib36) is a particularly
challenging subset of GPQA consisting of expert-written questions in
biology, physics, and chemistry that are designed to require domain
expertise and resist superficial answer retrieval. We report exact-match
accuracy using the benchmark’s flexible answer-extraction procedure,
which extracts the selected answer option from the generated response.

##### AGIEval English.

AGIEval English [Zhong et al. (2024)](#bib.bib37) evaluates general and
professional reasoning on English-language examination questions drawn
from several standardized and professional examinations. We report
accuracy, where a response is correct when the predicted answer matches
the reference answer.

##### IFEval.

IFEval [Zhou et al. (2023)](#bib.bib38) evaluates whether a model
follows objectively verifiable instructions that impose constraints on
the form or content of its response. We report prompt-level strict
accuracy, under which a response is correct only if it satisfies every
verifiable instruction associated with the prompt.

##### GSM8K.

GSM8K [Cobbe et al. (2021)](#bib.bib39) evaluates multi-step arithmetic
reasoning on grade-school mathematics word problems. We report strict
exact-match accuracy after extracting and normalizing the final numeric
answer from the generated response.

##### Minerva Math.

Minerva Math [Lewkowycz et al. (2022)](#bib.bib40) evaluates
mathematical problem solving on technical problems spanning multiple
mathematical subjects. We report mathematical-verification accuracy,
which considers a response correct when its extracted final answer is
mathematically equivalent to the reference answer.

##### HumanEval-Instruct.

HumanEval-Instruct [Chen et al. (2021)](#bib.bib41) evaluates
instruction-following code generation on programming problems whose
generated solutions are executed against unit tests. We report pass@1,
where a generated solution is correct if it passes all unit tests for
the problem.

##### MBPP-Instruct.

MBPP-Instruct [Odena et al. (2021)](#bib.bib42) evaluates
instruction-following code generation on short programming problems with
test cases defining the expected behavior. We report pass@1, where a
generated solution is correct if it passes all test cases for the
problem.

### D.4 Agentic-Capability Evaluation

We evaluate agentic capabilities to measure whether the defense methods
preserve the models’ ability to use tools and complete tasks in
interactive environments. For each agentic-capability benchmark, we
report the micro-averaged success rate over its elementary evaluation
units, such that every conversation, multi-turn entry, workplace task,
mission, or subtask receives equal weight.

##### ToolTalk.

ToolTalk [Farn and Shin (2023)](#bib.bib43) evaluates an assistant’s
ability to use APIs correctly in multi-turn conversations. Conversations
require the model to select appropriate tools, provide the required
arguments, and execute sequences of tool calls as the interaction
evolves; the benchmark includes 28 tools grouped into seven application
domains. We report conversation success rate. A conversation is
successful when the model recalls every reference tool call and makes no
incorrect action-tool call over the complete conversation.

##### BFCL Multi-Turn.

The Berkeley Function-Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) [Patil et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib44) evaluates function-calling capabilities across a
broad range of tool-use settings. We evaluate its multi_turn_base
subset, in which each entry may require multiple turns and multiple tool
calls against a stateful environment. We report entry-level accuracy: an
entry is correct only if the model’s tool calls across all turns satisfy
BFCL’s official multi-turn checker, including selection of the required
functions and construction of valid arguments.

##### WorkBench.

WorkBench [Styles et al. (2024)](#bib.bib45) evaluates whether
language-model agents can complete realistic workplace tasks by
interacting with software tools in a sandboxed environment. Tasks
include activities such as sending emails and scheduling meetings and
often require planning and executing multiple tool calls that modify the
underlying environment state. We report task-completion accuracy. A task
is successful when the model’s executed actions leave the sandbox in the
reference final state.

##### Multi-Mission Tool Bench.

Multi-Mission Tool Bench [Yu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib46) evaluates agents
on test cases containing sequences of interrelated missions whose
requirements evolve over the course of a conversation. Missions may
require single- or multi-tool execution, clarification of missing
parameters, or direct responses, and later missions can depend on
information established earlier in the interaction. We report
parameter-inclusive mission accuracy. A mission is successful when its
tool calls follow a valid path in the benchmark’s dynamic decision tree
and their arguments satisfy the official parameter checker.

##### AsyncTool.

AsyncTool [Shi et al. (2026)](#bib.bib47) evaluates tool-use agents in
asynchronous multi-task settings in which tool responses may be delayed.
The agent must coordinate several concurrent tasks, track dependencies
and intermediate states, and continue making progress on other tasks
while awaiting tool results. We report final subtask accuracy. A subtask
is successful when both its tool-call trajectory and its resulting
environment configuration are correct according to the official scorer.

### D.5 Agentic Prompt-Injection Evaluation

Agentic prompt-injection evaluation is central to this work, as it
measures whether a model can resist malicious instructions embedded in
tool outputs while still completing the user’s intended task. We
evaluate this security–utility trade-off using benchmarks that combine
interactive tool use, adversarially injected instructions, and
task-level success criteria. For each benchmark, we follow its official
aggregation convention. InjecAgent and AgentDojo aggregate over their
benchmark-defined evaluation cases, so that each test case (or sampled
attack, where applicable) receives equal weight. AgentDyn instead first
computes each metric separately for its Shopping, GitHub, and Daily Life
suites and reports the unweighted mean of the three suite-level scores.

##### InjecAgent.

InjecAgent [Zhan et al. (2024)](#bib.bib49) evaluates the vulnerability
of tool-integrated agents to indirect prompt injections embedded in
external content such as emails or webpages. Its 1,054 test cases span
17 user tools and 62 attacker tools, with malicious instructions
designed either to cause direct harm to the user or to exfiltrate
private information observed by the agent during task execution. The
agent must continue carrying out the benign user request while ignoring
the injected objective. We report total attack success rate separately
for the Base and Enhanced settings. In direct-harm cases, an attack
succeeds when the agent calls the attacker’s target tool; in
data-stealing cases, it succeeds when the agent completes both stages
and supplies the targeted private information to that tool.

##### AgentDojo.

AgentDojo [Debenedetti et al. (2024)](#bib.bib14) evaluates agents on
realistic tool-use tasks in domains such as workspace management, online
banking, travel booking, and messaging. Prompt injections are placed in
untrusted data returned by tools, for example in emails, documents, or
other environment content, and attempt to redirect the agent toward a
separate attacker-specified goal, such as leaking information or
performing an unauthorized action. The benchmark jointly measures
whether the agent completes the original user task and whether the
injected attacker objective succeeds. We report clean utility ($`U`$),
the fraction of benign user tasks completed without an attack; utility
under attack ($`U_{\mathrm{atk}}`$), the fraction of security cases in
which the original user task is completed; and targeted attack success
rate (ASR), the fraction of security cases in which the attacker’s
objective is achieved.

##### AgentDyn.

AgentDyn [Li et al. (2026)](#bib.bib17) extends agentic prompt-injection
evaluation to more open-ended and dynamically planned tasks across
Shopping, GitHub, and Daily Life scenarios. Its tasks require
longer-horizon interaction and may contain legitimate third-party
instructions that the agent should follow, making it necessary to
distinguish helpful external instructions from malicious injections.
Adversarial instructions are embedded in third-party content encountered
during the trajectory and attempt to divert the agent from the user’s
intended objective while it continues interacting with the environment.
We report clean utility ($`U`$), the fraction of user tasks completed
without an attack; utility under attack ($`U_{atk}`$), the fraction of
attacked cases in which the original user task is completed; and attack
success rate (ASR), the fraction of attacked cases in which the
malicious objective is achieved.

### D.6 Qwen: Additional Low-ASR Stress Test

from the primary experiments. Its Vanilla checkpoint already exhibits

whether RAISED remains effective when the starting model is already
comparatively resistant to prompt injection. We evaluate the same three
dimensions as in the main paper: prompt-injection robustness, benign
agentic capabilities, and general capabilities.

### D.7 Looking Inside the Model

RAISED trains the model to match its clean-context behavior when an
injection is added. We therefore ask whether the trained model shows
less internal sensitivity to the injection while remaining close to the
base model on clean inputs.

We evaluate this on 88 clean/injected context pairs from AgentDojo. For
each pair, we run the base model on the clean context to obtain its
continuation $`y^{\star}`$, then compare model states while reading the
clean and injected contexts followed by the same continuation. At each
of the 48 decoder blocks, we measure the injection-induced change in the
hidden state, as well as the distance between each trained model and the
base model on the clean context.

denotes the state after the final norm.

The injection produces a similar pattern across models in the early
blocks, followed by a peak around block 31. At that block, the relative
$`L_{2}`$ change is 0.45 for the base model, compared with 0.23 for
RAISED. This reduction goes with the behavioral check: RAISED starts the
injected tool call in 12.5% of the checked pairs, versus 62.5% for the
base model.

RAISED also remains closer to the base model on clean contexts than
SecAlign++ (0.12 vs. 0.19 at block 47). Thus, the internal-state
measurements are consistent with the intended behavior of the objective:
reduce sensitivity to injected content while limiting changes to
clean-context behavior.

### D.8 SecAlign++ training-step trade-off

The SecAlign++ results reported in the main paper use checkpoints
obtained after 313 training steps. The effect of extending training
differs across model families. On Gemma and Qwen, further training
primarily reduces utility without materially improving robustness. On
Nemotron, it further reduces attack success but comes with substantial
utility degradation. We use Nemotron below as a representative
illustration because the trade-off is particularly clear. We compare the
313-step checkpoint used in the main paper with the same model trained
for 625 steps, and include both the Vanilla checkpoint and RAISED as
reference points.

Table [12](#A4.T12 "Table 12 ‣ D.8 SecAlign++ training-step trade-off ‣ Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")
shows that additional SecAlign++ training continues to improve
robustness. On AgentDojo, ASR decreases from $`4.0\pm 0.7`$% at 313
steps to $`0.7\pm 0.0`$% at 625 steps, while on AgentDyn it decreases
from $`7.8\pm 0.3`$% to $`3.0\pm 0.2`$%. Thus, considering the security
benchmarks alone would suggest that further training is beneficial.

The benign agentic benchmarks show a milder version of the same effect.
For Nemotron, extending SecAlign++ training from 313 to 625 steps
reduces ToolTalk from $`43.2\pm 0.6`$ to $`42.7\pm 0.6`$, BFCL from
$`33.0\pm 0.4`$ to $`31.8\pm 0.8`$, MMT-Bench from $`43.4\pm 0.3`$ to
$`41.9\pm 0.3`$, and AsyncTool from $`34.5\pm 0.3`$ to $`32.3\pm 0.8`$,
while WorkBench increases. The main effect of prolonged training is
therefore not a uniform collapse of agentic performance, but a broader
and increasingly uneven drift away from the capabilities of the original
checkpoint.

These results explain our choice of the 313-step SecAlign++ checkpoint
for the main comparison. SecAlign++ can be trained longer to obtain
lower ASR, but selecting a checkpoint solely according to attack success
can conceal substantial degradation elsewhere. The same qualitative
training-duration trade-off is observed for Gemma and Qwen, although the
magnitude and affected capabilities differ across models. Nemotron
provides a particularly clear illustration of this phenomenon. In
contrast, RAISED reaches low attack success while remaining
substantially closer to the capability profile of the original model.

## Appendix E Ablation Study

The main comparison preserves SecAlign++’s original fine-tuning data
source, preference-data construction, and input representation,
providing the appropriate method-level comparison. However, RAISED
differs from SecAlign++ in both its training objective and training
data.

##### Controlled comparison.

As an alternative to our self-generated data, we use trajectories from
Glaive Function Calling v2, a synthetic function-calling dataset
containing tool specifications and multi-turn interactions. For each
clean Glaive trajectory, we construct an injected counterpart by taking
an instruction from a different Glaive example and inserting it into a
randomly selected tool output. The injected instruction is therefore
unrelated to the original user task, while the underlying trajectory
remains unchanged.

To isolate the training objective, we hold the trajectories, injection
placements, and rendered inputs fixed and compare SFT, DPO, and
self-distillation. For DPO, we follow the preference construction of
SecAlign++. The frozen base model generates the preferred response from
the clean Glaive context and the rejected response separately from the
injection itself, mirroring SecAlign++’s construction of preferred and
rejected responses from the clean input and injected instruction,
respectively. Both responses are then evaluated under the resulting
injected context by the DPO objective.

To isolate the effect of the training data, we then hold the objective
fixed and compare Glaive trajectories with the self-generated
trajectories used by RAISED, for both DPO and self-distillation.

|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | AgentDojo |  | AgentDyn |  |
| Data | Objective | $`U\uparrow`$ | ASR$`\downarrow`$ | $`U\uparrow`$ | ASR$`\downarrow`$ |
| – | Vanilla | 84.5 | 39.5 | 61.7 | 53.4 |
| Glaive | SFT | $`73.2{\pm}3.6`$ | $`0.5{\pm}0.3`$ | $`17.5{\pm}3.5`$ | $`1.5{\pm}1.2`$ |
| Glaive | DPO | $`79.1{\pm}0.6`$ | $`1.8{\pm}0.1`$ | $`48.6{\pm}0.3`$ | $`2.3{\pm}1.5`$ |
| Glaive | Self-distillation | $`80.1{\pm}0.6`$ | $`1.1{\pm}0.2`$ | $`55.5{\pm}0.8`$ | $`2.1{\pm}1.3`$ |
| Self-generated | DPO | $`82.2{\pm}0.5`$ | $`1.0{\pm}0.1`$ | $`55.6{\pm}3.4`$ | $`1.6{\pm}1.4`$ |
| Self-generated | Self-distillation (RAISED) | $`83.5{\pm}0.8`$ | $`1.0{\pm}0.3`$ | $`60.0{\pm}2.4`$ | $`1.6{\pm}1.8`$ |

Table 14: Ablation of training data and objective on Gemma-4-12B-it.
Higher is better for benign utility ($`U`$); lower is better for attack
success rate (ASR). Trained variants report mean$`\pm`$standard
deviation over three seeds.

##### Effect of the training objective.

Holding the Glaive data fixed, self-distillation preserves substantially
more benign agentic utility than SFT or DPO while maintaining low ASR.
On AgentDojo, self-distillation reaches $`80.1`$ utility, compared with
$`79.1`$ for DPO and $`73.2`$ for SFT. The difference is larger on
AgentDyn, where self-distillation reaches $`55.5`$, compared with
$`48.6`$ for DPO and $`17.5`$ for SFT. SFT attains slightly lower ASR
than self-distillation, but at a much larger utility cost, while
self-distillation also substantially improves robustness over DPO on
AgentDyn.

The self-generated data provide a second controlled comparison between
DPO and self-distillation. Both reach an AgentDojo ASR of $`1.0`$ and an
AgentDyn ASR of $`1.6`$ within the reported variation, while
self-distillation increases benign utility from $`82.2`$ to $`83.5`$ on
AgentDojo and from $`55.6`$ to $`60.0`$ on AgentDyn. Thus, with the data
and inputs held fixed, clean-context distribution matching preserves
more of the base model’s agentic behavior than the DPO objective used by
SecAlign++.

##### Effect of self-generation.

Holding the objective fixed shows an additional utility benefit from the
self-generated trajectories. With DPO, replacing Glaive with
self-generated data increases benign utility from $`79.1`$ to $`82.2`$
on AgentDojo and from $`48.6`$ to $`55.6`$ on AgentDyn, while reducing
ASR from $`1.8`$ to $`1.0`$ and from $`2.3`$ to $`1.6`$, respectively.

Self-distillation shows the same utility trend. Replacing Glaive with
self-generated trajectories increases utility from $`80.1`$ to $`83.5`$
on AgentDojo and from $`55.5`$ to $`60.0`$ on AgentDyn, while
maintaining low ASR. The benefit of self-generation therefore remains
when the training objective is held fixed.

##### Role of the structural patterns.

To test whether the gain from self-generated data comes from
self-generation alone or from the way generation is steered, we repeat
the experiment with the high-level structural patterns disabled while
keeping the rest of the generation pipeline unchanged. Benign utility
falls from $`83.5`$ to $`80.8{\pm}0.4`$ on AgentDojo and from $`60.0`$
to $`56.7{\pm}2.1`$ on AgentDyn, close to the $`80.1`$ and $`55.5`$
obtained with Glaive trajectories under self-distillation. This
indicates that the benefit of self-generation comes largely from
targeting scenarios that exercise the behaviors we aim to preserve,
rather than from synthetic data generation alone.

##### Summary.

The ablation supports both components of RAISED. With identical data and
inputs, self-distillation preserves more agentic utility than SFT or the
DPO objective used by SecAlign++ at similarly low attack success.
Holding the objective fixed, the self-generated trajectories provide a
further utility gain. RAISED combines these two effects.

## Appendix F Adaptive attacks

Our threat model considers static indirect prompt injections, in which
the adversarial content is chosen independently of the defended model
(Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Threat Model ‣ 3 Problem Formulation and Threat Model ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents")).
This setting matches the evaluation protocol of InjecAgent, AgentDojo,
and AgentDyn, and is the setting for which the robustness claims in this
work are made. In contrast, an adaptive attacker repeatedly queries a
particular defended model and optimizes the injected content against its
observed behavior. Such attacks grant the adversary an additional
capability and evaluate a distinct question: whether a defense remains
robust when the adversary can specialize its attack to that defense. We
nevertheless investigated this stronger setting using PISmith ([Yin et
al., 2026](#bib.bib50)), a recent black-box framework that optimizes
prompt injections against the target model. Using the authors’ released
code and protocol, however, the optimization reward remained identically
zero for most model–defense configurations. Consequently, the optimizer
received no signal with which to distinguish or improve candidate
attacks. This is consistent with the reward-sparsity regime discussed by
PISmith, but, importantly, a failed optimization run is not evidence of
adaptive robustness. We therefore do not report these runs as a
robustness result. Obtaining a more informative signal would require
modifying PISmith’s protocol, which falls outside the scope of this
work. We thus restrict our empirical robustness claims to the static
threat model defined in
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Threat Model ‣ 3 Problem Formulation and Threat Model ‣ RAISED: Self-Distillation for Robustness to Prompt Injection in LLM Agents").
Robustness to model-adaptive prompt injection remains an open question.

## Appendix G Limitations

##### Model scale and diversity.

We evaluate clean-context self-distillation on three model families with
different tokenizers, post-training recipes, and baseline robustness.
The consistency of the effect across Gemma, Nemotron and Qwen suggests
that it is not specific to one family, and the objective itself makes no
architecture-specific assumption. We have not yet evaluated additional
model families or frontier models in the trillion-parameter regime, so
whether the same security–utility behavior persists at that scale
remains an empirical question.

##### Dependence on clean-model behavior.

Clean-context self-distillation preserves the model’s own behavior; it
does not improve its correctness. If the clean model selects the wrong
tool, follows a poor plan, hallucinates, or otherwise behaves
undesirably, the distillation objective will preserve that behavior
under injection rather than correct it. The quality of the defended
model is therefore bounded by the quality of the clean-context teacher.
The method should be understood as a defence against adversarial context
influence, not as a general alignment or safety intervention.

##### Cost of soft self-distillation.

Soft self-distillation requires an offline teacher pass and storage of
truncated predictive distributions. For our 10,000-trace corpus, storing
the top-256 teacher distributions requires approximately 15 GB per
model, and teacher generation completes in well under one hour using
eight parallel inference workers on our GB200 cluster. At frontier
scale, the teacher pass becomes substantially more expensive: a model
such as Kimi K3 activates roughly 104B parameters per token,
approximately $`4\times`$ to $`9\times`$ the active parameter count of
the dense models evaluated here.

## Appendix H Broader Impact

Indirect prompt injection is a practical obstacle to deploying
language-model agents over untrusted external content. Clean-context
self-distillation may improve the reliability of agents operating over
web pages, documents, emails, APIs, and other external data sources
while retaining their useful tool-use behavior. The method should be
viewed as a defence-in-depth mechanism that complements access control,
sandboxing, capability restrictions, and other system-level safeguards
````
